newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels defiant after freeing ill police chief.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels defiant after freeing ill police chief.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding scores of hostages freed an ailing police commander on Sunday -- their first release in nine days -- but vowed to continue the 40-day standoff until the Peruvian government met their demands.

Gen. Jose Rivas Rodriguez, a deputy chief in the Peruvian national police, was wheeled out of the besieged Japanese ambassador's compound in the early hours on a hospital gurney flanked by Red Cross officials and Bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
Lying face up with his bare feet sticking out from under a blanket, Rodriguez was taken to an ambulance and driven to a nearby police hospital.
International Committee of the Red Cross representative Michel Minnig said the rebels agreed to free Rodriguez on medical grounds. He was suffering from stress, Minnig said.
In the previous release on Jan. 17, the rebels freed another police chief for medical reasons. The two officials are the only men to have been freed since New Year's Day.
There seemed little prospect, however, of an early release for the remaining 72 captives held by the heavily armed Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
The Red Cross said the remaining hostages were in good health.

"The situation is calm. Given the circumstances, I think they are all well," Red Cross official Ruben Ortega told local radio station, RPP, adding that doctors were regularly tending to captives' "particular medical needs."

The Red Cross has repeatedly said the hostages were in stable health, despite claims from their relatives and colleagues that some were sick. The rebels have said the health of their captives is "under control."
Shortly after dawn on Sunday, the MRTA rebels made the now daily broadcast of their revolutionary hymn from inside the residence and shouted that they would not surrender.
"We've been here for 40 days and we are going to continue resisting," an unidentified rebel shouted through a megaphone.
Rodriguez's release followed several days of tense posturing, with rebels firing warning shots into the air on Saturday in response to what they called provocative movements by the police outside.

As part of the sometimes bizarre psychological games between the police and guerrillas, two special forces officers signalled on Sunday to a female rebel at a window to leave the residence and join them on the street. In reply, she gestured that, instead, the men join her inside.
Police staking out the diplomatic mansion have thrown stones and trash into the grounds and boarded up a side door in the perimeter wall.

Armoured vehicles have twice rumbled past the residence, a police helicopter has flown overhead and troops armed with high-powered weapons and night-vision equipment have rushed the main entrance, their rifles pointed at the building.
The helicopter returned to the site on Sunday, but kept further away from the compound than in previous days.

The leader of Peru's Roman Catholic Church, Cardinal Augusto Vargas Alzamora, accompanied Cipriani on a half-hour visit to the hostages on Sunday. Emerging from the residence, Vargas called for divine intervention to bring a breakthrough.
"Men sometimes do not find a solution ... now we need God to intervene," he told reporters to the sound of Lima church bells chiming in the distance.

Government negotiator Domingo Palermo said on Saturday he had held a preliminary meeting with a commission of "guarantors" who will oversee eventual peace talks. "The Red Cross is preparing for the MRTA to eventually come out for the start of conversations," he said. "I am going to be very clear. There is no deadlock."

About 100 Japanese tourists, members of the non- governmental "Peace Boat", arrived at the siege site early on Sunday. They carried banners in the shape of hearts and brought hundreds of origami sculptures for the hostages.
The rebels took more than 500 hostages on Dec. 17 when they stormed a cocktail party at the diplomatic mansion, but have freed most of them in what they called "goodwill gestures."

The remaining captives in the mined and booby-trapped residence include two Peruvian ministers, congressmen, judges, police and army chiefs, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
